books.section: Topic 6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

options.text: They faced the same falling wages and pay cuts in the same depression.

options.misconception: The passage says workers followed, not that a governor ordered them to.
options.text: The governor of West Virginia ordered every railroad worker to stop work at once.

options.misconception: Hayes sent troops to end the strike, not to order one.
options.text: President Hayes himself ordered every railroad worker everywhere to strike.

options.misconception: The passage says the railroad cut pay; it never says it paid workers to strike.
options.text: The Baltimore and Ohio paid its own workers to spread the strike.

rationales.A: The passage sets the strike in a depression of falling wages, so workers elsewhere shared the same grievance and followed.
rationales.B: The passage says workers followed, not that a governor ordered them to.
rationales.C: Hayes sent troops to end the strike, not to order one.
rationales.D: The passage says the railroad cut pay; it never says it paid workers to strike.
rationales.general:
Use the background the passage gives.
1. Wages had already fallen in the depression after the Panic of 1873.
2. Then the Baltimore and Ohio announced a further 10 percent cut.
3. Railroad workers in other cities lived under the same depression and the same cuts.
4. So they followed Martinsburg because they shared the grievance.
Remember: a shared grievance explains a spread better than an order nobody gave.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: The passage says wages had already fallen during the depression after the Panic of 1873. Given that background, why did workers in Pittsburgh and Chicago follow the Martinsburg strikers?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage, written for this question from Barron’s Premium 2027 Chapter 8 (Topic 6.7), 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 18, and Princeton Review, Chapter 10.
stimulus.text:
Original secondary passage, written for this question from the grounding books:

In July 1877, the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad announced a 10 percent pay cut for its workers, whose wages had already fallen during the depression that followed the Panic of 1873. Railroad workers in Martinsburg, West Virginia, stopped the trains, and workers in Pittsburgh, Chicago, and other cities followed. At its height the strike involved more than 100,000 railroad workers. Violence broke out in nine states, and President Rutherford B. Hayes sent federal troops to end the strike. The troops Hayes sent had recently been withdrawn from enforcing Reconstruction in the South.
